claim: Text-to-SQL fails silently and confidently; output may look right even when wrong, e.g. an LLM interprets FRT as First Resolution Time instead of First Response Time and the SQL runs with plausible numbers but measures the wrong thing.
quote: The real danger is that text-to-SQL fails silently and confidently. The output may look right, even if it's wrong... picks a random timestamp column. The SQL runs and the numbers look fine. They measure the wrong thing.

claim: Wrong join paths return the wrong metric: asking for MRR by product line, the LLM joins orders directly to products and returns total order value instead of recurring revenue.
quote: A business user asks for MRR (monthly recurring revenue) by product line. The LLM joins orders directly to products, skipping the subscription model. The result returned is total order value, not recurring revenue.

claim: Catching a semantically-wrong query requires reading and understanding the generated SQL, which demands the same expertise the tool was meant to replace.
quote: Catching the error requires reading the generated SQL and understanding it, the same expertise the tool was supposed to replace.

claim: A query about monthly retention executed correctly but interpreted 'month' as elapsed days from each user's first purchase rather than the calendar-month boundaries the business used, so the result silently meant something different from what was asked.
quote: The model interpreted "month" as elapsed days from each user's first purchase, when the business actually defined it using calendar month boundaries. The query executed correctly but the number on the slide just means something different from what the analyst typed.

claim: Business definitions like 'star product', 'loyal customer', and 'active account' live in people's heads or stale docs; a general LLM picks the most statistically similar interpretation, rarely the one finance actually uses.
quote: 'Star product.' 'Loyal customer.' 'Active account.' A general-purpose LLM picks the most statistically similar interpretation, which is rarely the one your finance team uses on Monday mornings.

claim: 'Confident-but-wrong' is the failure mode that audit and compliance teams flag, because the model interpolates underspecified intent with the most statistically-likely interpretation rather than the business's actual definition.
quote: the model interpolates the hole with the most statistically-likely interpretation from its training data, and that interpretation is rarely how your business defines anything... 'Confident-but-wrong' is the failure mode that audit and compliance teams flag.

claim: In a 2026 benchmark, text-to-SQL on modeled data reached 90.0% (Claude Sonnet 4.6) and 84.1% (GPT-5.3 Codex) vs 98.2%/100% via a semantic layer; on the full question set raw text-to-SQL was only 64.5%.
quote: Text-to-SQL accuracy nearly doubled, from 32.7% to 64.5% on the full question set.

claim: The dangerous asymmetry: text-to-SQL failure looks like a plausible but incorrect answer while a semantic layer fails with an error message, and text-to-SQL will 'cheerfully give you a wrong number'.
quote: With text-to-SQL, failure looks like a plausible but incorrect answer. With the Semantic Layer, failure looks like an error message... Text-to-SQL will cheerfully give you a wrong number.

claim: NL2SQL is inherently hard because the natural-language question is ambiguous (lexical, syntactic, semantic, schema-linking, and intent ambiguity) while SQL requires precise understanding of schema and semantics.
quote: NL2SQL is challenging in that the natural language question is inherently ambiguous, while the SQL generation requires a precise understanding of complex data schema and semantics.

claim: Aggregate functions SUM/AVG/COUNT(col)/MAX/MIN silently ignore NULLs (only COUNT(*) counts NULL rows), so an AVG over a column with NULLs is computed over fewer rows than the user assumes.
quote: NULL values are not considered in any aggregate function like SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MAX() and MIN(), with the exception being the COUNT(*) function, which counts all rows, even those rows with NULL values.

claim: A JOIN fan-out occurs when a one-to-many/many-to-many join multiplies rows, causing COUNT and SUM to silently double-count and return inflated aggregates from a query that runs without error.
quote: A fanout occurs when the primary table in a query contains fewer rows than the combined table resulting from a JOIN. Because the new table contains more rows, aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM may include duplicates, throwing off the results.

claim: Date-range BETWEEN is inclusive and silently drops rows with a time component after midnight on the end date; experts recommend semi-open intervals (>= start AND < next-period-start) to avoid off-by-one and timezone errors.
quote: A row that contains a time part that is after 12:00 A.M. on January 5, 2002, isn't returned by this query, because it falls outside the range.
